milestones.title: Catch every byte: ring buffer and RX interrupt
milestones.body:
**The ring buffer** (`src/ringbuf.c`). Bytes arrive in an interrupt and are consumed later by the main loop, so they need somewhere to wait. Implement the four functions in `ringbuf.h`:

- `rb_init` sets a ring up over storage the caller owns (no `malloc`). The size must be a power of two and at least 2. Anything else returns `false`.
- `rb_put` is the producer side, only ever called from the interrupt. When the ring is full it **drops the new byte**, counts it in `dropped` and returns `false`. It never waits.
- `rb_get` is the consumer side, only ever called from the main loop. It hands out the oldest byte, or returns `false` when there's nothing.
- A ring of size N holds at most N − 1 bytes, so full and empty look different without a shared count.
- No locks and no disabling interrupts: the interrupt may fire between any two lines of `rb_get`, and nothing may break when it does.

**The RX interrupt handler** (`src/uart.c`). `uart_init` sets up a ring of `UART_RX_SIZE` bytes in static storage and zeroes the counters. `uart_rx_isr` is what the hardware calls when a byte has arrived:

1. If `RXNE` isn't set in `SR`, the interrupt wasn't for us: return without touching anything.
2. If `ORE` is set, count an overrun (`uart_overruns`).
3. Take the byte from the low 8 bits of `DR` and put it in the ring.
4. Clear `RXNE` and `ORE` by writing 0 to those two bits, and leave every other bit of `SR` as it was.

`uart_getc` and `uart_rx_dropped` are the main loop's view of the same ring.

**Done when** `make test-m1` is green.
hints: Picture the interrupt stopping rb_get halfway, between any two of its lines, and running rb_put to the end. Which variables does each side write? If only one side ever writes a given index, what's the worst the other side can see?

This is the lock-free SPSC ring from Interrupts & ring buffers: head belongs to the producer, tail to the consumer, and a power-of-two size turns the wrap-around into a mask instead of a division. Clearing two flags without touching their neighbours is the read-modify-write from Bits & registers, on a volatile register as in Memory-mapped I/O & volatile.

Put: work out the slot after head. If that's tail, the ring is full, so count the drop and give up. Otherwise store the byte first and move head last. Get: if tail equals head it's empty. Otherwise read the byte at tail, then move tail. Count is the distance from tail to head, masked. The ISR reads SR once into a local, checks RXNE, then ORE, reads DR, clears the two flags and hands the byte to put.

milestones.title: From bytes to lines: the line editor
milestones.body:
Turn the byte stream into lines, the way a serial terminal expects. `line_feed` gets one character at a time and returns an event (see `line.h`). It's a state machine: `line_t` has a `state`, and the three states are already named.

- A printable character (space to `~`) is added to the line and **echoed** with `out_putc`. A serial terminal shows only what the device sends back, so without the echo you'd type blind.
- `\r` or `\n` finishes the line: echo `\r\n` and return `LINE_READY`. `line_get` then returns the line as a string. Enter on an empty line is a `LINE_READY` with an empty line.
- Terminals send `\r`, `\n` or `\r\n` for Enter. A `\n` that comes **straight after** a `\r` belongs to the same Enter and is ignored. Two `\r` in a row are two Enters.
- Backspace arrives as `0x7F` (most terminals) or `\b`. It removes the last character and echoes `\b \b` (back, overwrite with a space, back again). On an empty line it does nothing and echoes nothing.
- Any other byte (tab, escape, other control bytes, anything above `0x7E`) is ignored and not echoed.
- A line holds at most `LINE_MAX` (32) characters. A printable character beyond that puts the editor into overflow: from then on nothing is stored or echoed, backspaces included, until Enter, which echoes `\r\n` and returns `LINE_TOO_LONG`. The next line starts fresh.

Example: typing `l` `e` `x` Backspace `d` Enter echoes `lex\b \bd\r\n` and gives the line `led`.

**Done when** `make test-m2` is green.
hints: For each of the three states, what does each kind of input do: printable, Enter, backspace, anything else? Which combinations change the state, and which only change the buffer? A small table on paper first saves a lot of debugging.

This is the enum and switch state machine from Superloops & state machines: every state answers every input, only here the input is a character instead of a tick. The buffer is a fixed array inside line_t, as in Memory without malloc, so the length check before every store is the only thing keeping it in bounds.

Switch on the state. After a carriage return, swallow a newline and go back to collecting; anything else is handled exactly as in collecting. Collecting: Enter terminates the string, resets the length for the next line, echoes and reports ready, remembering whether it was a carriage return. Backspace shrinks the length if there is one. Printable characters are stored and echoed while there's room, and the first one without room switches to overflow. Overflow: ignore everything until Enter, then report too long.

milestones.title: A shell: split, dispatch, prompt
milestones.body:
Now make it a shell. The signatures are in `shell.h` and `commands.h`.

- **`shell_split`** cuts a line into words **in place**. Separators (any run of spaces and tabs) are skipped, the end of each word becomes `\0`, and `argv` points into the line. It returns the number of words, or -1 when there are more than `max_args`.
- **`shell_exec`** runs one line and leaves it unmodified: it looks the first word up in the `shell_commands` table, calls that entry's handler with `argc` and `argv`, and returns what the handler returns. The cases that never reach a command:
  - a blank line prints nothing and returns 0
  - longer than `LINE_MAX`: `error: line too long (max 32)`
  - more than `SHELL_MAX_ARGS` words: `error: too many arguments`
  - no such command: `unknown command: <first word>`

  Each message ends in `\r\n` and the result is -1.
- **The first commands** are already in the table. You write them:
  - `help` prints one row per table entry, in table order: the name padded with spaces to 8 characters, then its help text. Adding a row to the table is all it takes for a command to show up.
  - `echo a   b` prints `a b`: the words after `echo`, separated by single spaces. `echo` alone prints an empty line.
  - `stats` prints `rx dropped 8, overruns 1` with the two UART counters.
- **`shell_init`** starts the UART and the line editor and prints `uart-shell ready\r\n> `.
- **`shell_poll`** is the main loop's turn: it handles every byte waiting in the UART. A finished line runs and is followed by the prompt `> `. A too-long line prints the too-long error, then the prompt.

Every output line ends in `\r\n`. Then try it for real: `make run` and type `help`.

**Done when** `make test-m3` is green.
hints: Which part needs to know about which? Does the line editor need to know commands exist? Does help need a list of names, or can it find them out? And why does shell_exec need its own copy of the line before it splits it?

The table is a lookup by name: each row holds the name, the handler and the help text, and the handler field is a pointer whose type, cmd_fn_t, is given in shell.h. Calling through it looks like any other call. Splitting in place, into a buffer you own instead of new memory, is the no-malloc thinking from Memory without malloc.

Split: loop over the line. Skip separators and stop at the end. If you already have max words, report too many. Otherwise remember where this word starts, walk to its end and overwrite the separator there with a terminator. Exec: check the length, copy into a local array, split, handle the blank and too-many cases, then compare the first word with each table row and call the match. Poll: while the UART has a byte, feed it to the editor and act on ready or too long.

milestones.title: Drive the hardware: led, gpio, reg
milestones.body:
Give the shell something to control. First **`parse_u32`**: a number on the command line is either decimal (`42`, `007`) or hex with a `0x` or `0X` prefix (`0x2A`, `0xc0de0042`). Nothing else is a number: no sign, no spaces, no empty string or bare `0x`, no trailing junk, nothing above 4294967295. On failure it returns `false` and leaves `*out` alone. Leading zeros mean decimal here, unlike C's octal `010`.

Then add `led`, `gpio` and `reg` to the table and write them. The register map is in `periph.h` and the README. **Every change to a register leaves all its other bits exactly as they were.**

| Command | Does | Prints |
|---|---|---|
| `led on`, `led off` | sets or clears the `LED` bit of `CTRL` | `ok` |
| `led blink <n>` | writes n (0 to 15) into the `BLINK` field | `ok` |
| `led` | reads `CTRL` | `led on, blink 5` |
| `gpio set <pin>`, `gpio clear <pin>` | sets or clears that bit of `GPIO_OUT` | `ok` |
| `gpio get <pin>` | reads that bit of `GPIO_IN` | `gpio 7 = 1` |
| `reg read <off>` | reads the register at byte offset `off` | `0x04 = 0x00000021` |
| `reg write <off> <value>` | writes the whole register | `ok` |

Hex output is uppercase and zero-padded as shown: two digits for an offset, eight for a value. Errors, which change nothing:

- a blink rate outside 0 to 15, or not a number: `error: blink rate must be 0-15`
- a pin outside 0 to 15, or not a number: `error: pin must be 0-15`
- an offset that isn't a multiple of 4 inside the block, or not a number: `error: offset must be 0x00-0x0C in steps of 4`
- a value that isn't a number: `error: bad value`
- writing `GPIO_IN` or `ID`: `error: register 0x08 is read-only` (with that register's offset)
- any other form (unknown subcommand, wrong number of words) prints the command's usage: `usage: led [on|off|blink <0-15>]`, `usage: gpio set|clear|get <pin>` or `usage: reg read <offset> | reg write <offset> <value>`

Every line ends in `\r\n`. Success returns 0, every error non-zero. Have `reg` compute the register's address from the block's base and the offset, the way you'd poke any register on a real chip, rather than a `switch` over the four names.

**Done when** `make test-m4` is green, and so is the whole `make test`.
hints: Say CTRL holds 0xA5A50031 and someone types led blink 9. Write the before and after in binary on paper. Which bits must change, which must not, and why does simply OR-ing the new rate in give the wrong answer?

Changing one bit or one field and keeping the rest is set, clear, and field insert and extract from Bits & registers, using the _Pos and _Msk macros in periph.h. Turning a byte offset into a register pointer is base address plus offset from Memory-mapped I/O & volatile: add the offset to the address as an integer, then cast, or pointer arithmetic scales it by 4.

Parse: look for the 0x prefix, then walk the digits, building the value and refusing just before it would overflow; for decimal, compare against the maximum divided by ten first. Commands: check the form first and print usage if it's wrong, then parse and range-check the numbers, then do one read-modify-write of the register and print ok. For reg, validate the offset, refuse read-only registers on a write, and go through a volatile pointer made from hal_dev() plus the offset.

milestones.title: Optional: run it on a real board
milestones.body:
Optional, and nothing tests it. The last section of the starter's `README.md` walks through it. Replace `hal_host.c` and `main.c` with versions for a real board, keep `ringbuf.c`, `uart.c`, `line.c`, `shell.c` and `commands.c` **unchanged**, and talk to your shell over USB serial with `picocom`. The README has concrete steps for an STM32 Nucleo-F401RE, whose USART2 has the same `SR` and `DR` as our UART, and notes for a Raspberry Pi Pico, whose UART is different.

**Done when** `led on` typed into picocom lights the board's LED, and pasting a dozen commands at once runs them all (or, if you paste more than the ring holds, `stats` tells you exactly how many bytes were dropped).
hints: Which of your files use anything that only exists on a PC? If none outside hal_host.c, main.c and sim.h do, the port is mostly bring-up. What does the chip need before the first byte can even arrive?

Clocks, pin modes, alternate functions, the baud rate and the peripheral enable are the same register work as in Bits & registers and Memory-mapped I/O & volatile, only now the bit positions come from the reference manual instead of periph.h. Enabling the interrupt in the peripheral and in the NVIC is the part of Interrupts & ring buffers the simulator did for you. Our device block has no real twin, so keep it in RAM and mirror it to the LED: that's a HAL decision, not a core one.

Get the LED on from main first. Then send a banner by polling TXE. Then receive with the interrupt and echo each byte. Only then link in the shell. One new thing at a time, each checked before the next, so when something breaks you know which step broke it.
